title: Applying Cognitive Load Theory to Detect AI Deception via Response Latency and Complexity
original_idea: Elicit deceptive vs. honest responses. Measure response length, syntactic complexity, hedge words, clause depth. Train simple classifier. ~200 examples on single GPU.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: cognitive load markers as a post-hoc screening tool would be cheap and practical if they work. But the transfer of human cognitive load theory to LLMs is speculative.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very accessible: text feature extraction (length, complexity, hedge words) and simple classifier training on 200 examples. Perfect for CS students with basic ML knowledge. Single GPU is fine for medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: generate responses, extract features, train classifier. The 200-example target is realistic. Clear binary outcome (does the classifier work?). Feasible in 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: Research on cognitive load markers for deception detection is extensive in the human domain (Fallah et al., 2025 on pauses/hesitations; audio-visual cognitive load feature extraction). For LLM-generated text specifically, existing work has identified that cognitive load and perceptual-contextual details are powerful discriminators for both human and machine deception. LIWC-based linguistic analysis for deception is well-established. Fine-tuned BERT classifiers for deception detection achieve strong results. The specific application to LLM self-generated deception (not LLM-generated fake reviews) using response length, syntactic complexity, and hedge words as features for a classifier is partially novel, but the methodology closely parallels existing computational deception detection work.

evidence: Fallah et al. (2025). Cognitive Load as a Key to Lie Detection. SAGE Journals.
What if Deception Cannot be Detected? A Cross-Linguistic Study. arXiv:2505.13147, 2025.
SVM, BERT, or LLM? A Comparative Study on Multilingual Instructed Deception Detection. MDPI, 2025.
